chapter: Charlie Johnson, Willie Gant and the late 1920s
title: Indian ancestry in jazz musicians
summary: Caldwell and Dance discuss Native American heritage among musicians and in the South, citing Pettiford, Fats Navarro and his own grandfather.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Well, you say you thought he was part Indian or somebody --

Yeah, down on his grandfather's side, like my grandfather or great grandfather, yeah, because take all parts of the South and even upstate New York, up New Jersey, all up in Indian England reservations at the time, most all things of that sort of the South, particularly, and (unintelligible) --
You don't think -- you know, that people, some people at different times have said, you know,
they talk about jazz as a music created by black musicians, but sometimes people have said to me, well, there's a whole lot of Indian mixed up with that too.
That's true.
Do you think --

Offsprings, yeah, there is. Take this fellow, for instance, this guy Hendrix that died in London here about -- either London or Paris about three years ago. He was a rock singer. He died just before this girl Joplin. Well, he was part Cherokee Indian.
Yeah, well, I mean, you know, you hear quite a lot of jazz musicians whose, you know, mother or father -- wasn't Oscar Pettiford --
Oscar Pettiford? Part Cherokee from out of Oklahoma. [side note: tribe]
Well, it just seems it is possible, you know, when you stop to sort of think of music being influenced by race (unintelligible) or whatever, that the Indian thing is in there too.

Just like New Orleans, right across -- Algiers is all mixed up with East Indian, Indian and French. That's why they speak all that Patois. They don't speak the real Parisian French. They speak Patois French. That's the same way down in there. All through the South -- at one time before the Emancipation Proclamation was

instituted, when they were running the slaves here and there, a lot of the Indians accepted them. One of the biggest Indian chiefs, Osceola, in -- off the (unintelligible) in Key West in Florida, the Everglades, down through there, they never conquered those Indians, but the Indians made peace with them because they knew that land better than anybody else. And a lot of the offsprings, like this guy -- we had a guitar player. He was part Seminole, the Seminole tribe down there, and this boy played trumpet from out of Florida, he was part Seminole. They made quite a few records or a kick bebop came -- Fats Navarro.
Oh, yeah. Yeah.
He's part Seminole.
Yeah. Well, I mean it's very hard to, you know, when you come to music, to say what kind of heritage of blood or race or anything could do --
That's true.
-- but, nevertheless, that Indian thing could possibly, you know, if you could put it on a computer or something --
(Laughter)
-- you might find it -- they contributed quite a bit.
That's right, because a lot of the -- I'd say, for instance, background group -- those baggies, they got to be some of that. My grandpa was an old Indian
chief down there, Cherokee Indian chief. And the other one was a preacher.
